stab.e: Supposed by some to derive from Scottish Gaelic stob (“to prick, to prod, to push, to thrust”); supposed by others to be from a Scots word.
stab.g: An act of stabbing or thrusting with an object to hurt or kill someone.
The horizontal or vertical stabilizer of an aircraft.

stability.e: From Middle English stabletee, stabilite, from Old French stabilité, from Latin root of stabilitas (“firmness, steadfastness”), from stabilis (“steadfast, firm”).
stability.g: The condition of being stable or in equilibrium, and thus resistant to change.

stable.e: From Middle English stable, borrowed from Anglo-Norman stable, from Latin stab(u)lum. From Middle English stable, borrowed from Anglo-Norman stable, from Latin stab(u)lum.
stable.g: A building, wing or dependency set apart and adapted for lodging and feeding (and training) ungulates, especially horses.

stable.e: From Middle English stable, from Anglo-Norman stable, stabel, from Latin stabilis (“firm, steadfast”) (itself from stare (“stand”) + -abilis (“able”)).
stable.g: Relatively unchanging, steady, permanent; firmly fixed or established; consistent; not easily moved, altered, or destroyed.

stack.e: From Middle English stack, stacke, stakke, stak, from Old Norse stakkr (“a barn; haystack; heap; pile”), from Proto-Germanic *stakkaz (“a barn; rick; haystack”). The data structure sense is a calque of Dutch stapel, introduced by Edsger W. Dijkstra.

stacte.e: From Latin stactē, from Ancient Greek στακτή (staktḗ, “oil of myrrh”) from στακτός (staktós, “oozing out in drops”).
stacte.g: One of the sweet spices used by the Jews in Biblical times for preparing incense; it is thought to have been an oil or other form of myrrh o

stadia.e: From Ancient Greek στᾰ́δῐᾰ (stắdĭă), plural of στᾰ́δῐον (stắdĭon).

staff.e: From Middle English staf, from Old English stæf (“letter of the alphabet”), from Proto-West Germanic *stab, from Proto-Germanic *stabaz. Sense of "group of military officers that assists a commander" and similar meanings, attested from 1702, is influenced by or is even from German Stab.
staff.g: A long, straight, thick wooden rod or stick, especially one used to assist in walking.

stag.e: From Middle English stagge, steg, from Old English stagga, stacga (“a stag”) and possibly Old Norse steggi, steggr (“a male animal”), both from Proto-Germanic *staggijô, *staggijaz (“male, male deer, porcupine”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *stegʰ-, *stengʰ- (“to sting; rod, blade; sharp, stiff”).
stag.g: An adult male deer, especially a red deer and especially one in high adulthood versus a young adult.

stage.e: From Middle English stage, from Old French estage (“dwelling, residence; position, situation, condition”), from Old French ester (“to be standing, be located”).

stage.g: An unpaid internship in a restaurant where a cook or chef is exposed to new culinary techniques.

stagger.e: From Middle English stageren, a variant of stakeren ("to walk unsteadily, stagger"; whence modern dialectal English stacker (“to totter, reel, stagger”)), from Old Norse stakra (“to stagger, sway, waver, swing, wobble”), frequentative of Old Norse staka (“to push, knock, bump into, stumble”).
stagger.g: An unsteady movement of the body in walking or standing as if one were about to fall; a reeling motion.

stain.e: From Middle English steinen, steynen (“to stain, colour, paint”), of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse steina (“to stain, colour, paint”), from steinn (“stone, mineral blue, colour, stain”), from Proto-Norse ᛊᛏᚨᛁᚾᚨᛉ (stainaʀ), from Proto-Germanic *stainaz (“stone”), from Proto-Indo-European *steyh₂- (“to stiffen”).
stain.g: A discolored spot or area caused by spillage or other contact with certain fluids or substances.

stair.e: From Middle English steire, staire, stayre, stayer, steir, steyre, steyer, from Old English stǣġer (“stair, staircase”), from Proto-West Germanic *staigri, from Proto-Germanic *staigriz (“stairs, scaffolding”), from Proto-Indo-European *steygʰ- (“to walk, proceed, march, climb”).
stair.g: A single step in a staircase.

stake.e: From Middle English stake, from Old English staca (“pin, tack, stake”), from Proto-West Germanic *stakō, from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“stake”), from Proto-Indo-European *stog-, *steg- (“stake”).
stake.g: A piece of wood or other material, usually long and slender, pointed at one end so as to be easily driven into the ground as a marker or a s

stalk.e: From Middle English stalke, stelke, stalk, perhaps from Old English *stealc, *stielc, *stealuc, from Proto-West Germanic *staluk, *stalik, from Proto-Germanic *stalukaz, *stalikaz, diminutive of Proto-Germanic *stalô, *staluz (“support, stem, stalk”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to place, stand; be stiff; stud, post, trunk, stake, stem, stalk”).
stalk.g: The stem or main axis of a plant.

stalk.e: From Middle English stalken, from Old English *stealcian (as in bestealcian (“to move stealthily”), stealcung (“stalking”)), from Proto-West Germanic *stalukōn.
stalk.g: To approach slowly and quietly in order not to be discovered when getting closer.

stall.e: From Middle English stall, stalle, from Old English steall (“standing place, position”), from Proto-Germanic *stallaz, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to place, put, post, stand”).
stall.g: A compartment for a single animal in a stable or cattle shed.

stall.e: From Middle English stallen (“to abide, dwell, place in a location, stop, come to a standstill”), partly from Old French estaler, ultimately from the same origin as Etymology 1 (see above); and partly from Middle English stalle (“fixed position, stall”).
stall.g: An action that is intended to cause, or actually causes, delay.

stallion.e: From Middle English stalion, from Middle French estalon (whence modern French étalon), of Germanic origin, akin to stall.

stammer.e: From Middle English stameren, from Old English stamerian, from Proto-West Germanic *stamrōn, from Proto-Germanic *stamrōną (“to stammer”).
stammer.g: To keep repeating a particular sound involuntarily during speech.

stamp.e: From Middle English stampen (“to pound, crush”), from assumed Old English *stampian, variant of Old English stempan (“to crush, pound, pound in mortar, stamp”), from Proto-West Germanic *stampōn, *stampijan, from Proto-Germanic *stampōną, *stampijaną (“to trample, beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *stemb- (“to trample down”).
stamp.g: An act of stamping the foot, paw or hoof.

stanch.e: From Middle English stanch, a variant of staunch, staunche (“(adjective) in good condition or repair; solidly made, firm; watertight; of a person or wound: not bleeding; certain; intact; (adverb) firmly, soundly”); see further at staunch.

From Middle English stanch, stanche, a variant of Middle English staunchen, staunche (“to stop the flow of blood, diarrhoea, or other bodily fluids; to alleviate, ease; to appease, assuage, satisfy; to cure; to overcome; to put an end to; to repress, suppress; of a river or stream: to stop flowing; of waters, wind, or weather: to become calm, subside.
stanch.g: To stop the flow of (water or some other liquid).

stand.e: From Middle English stonden, standen (verb) and stand, stond (noun, from the verb), from Old English standan (“to stand, occupy a place”), from Proto-West Germanic *standan, from Proto-Germanic *standaną (“to stand”), from Pre-Germanic *sth₂-n-t-´, an innovative extended n-infixed form of Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-.
stand.g: To position or be positioned physically:

stand.e: From Middle English stand, stande, stond, stonde, stoonde, probably from Middle Dutch stande, from Old Dutch *standan (“to stand”), from Frankish *standan. Forms with -o- may show influence of stonden (“stand”, verb).
stand.g: A container which stands upright, such as a barrel or cask.

standard.e: From Middle English standard, from Old French estandart (“gathering place, battle flag”), from Frankish *standahard (literally “stand firm, stand hard”), equivalent to stand + -ard.
standard.g: Falling within an accepted range of size, amount, power, quality, etc.

standing.e: From Middle English standynge, stondynge, standende, stondinde, standande, stondande, from Old English standende, stondende, from Proto-Germanic *standandz (“standing”), present participle of Proto-Germanic *standaną (“to stand”), equivalent to stand + -ing.

standstill.e: From stand + still, a deverbal from stand still.

stank.e: Respelling of stink, representing the thank-think merger.
From Old French estanc, or Italian stanco.

star.e: From Middle English sterre, from Old English steorra (“star”), from Proto-West Germanic *sterrō, variant of *sternō, from Proto-Germanic *sternô, *sternǭ (“star”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr (“star”).
star.g: Any small, natural and bright dot in the sky, most visible in the night or twilight sky. This sense includes the planets, but it is now some

stare.e: From Middle English staren, from Old English starian (“to stare”), from Proto-West Germanic *starēn, from Proto-Germanic *starjaną, *starāną (“to be fixed, be rigid”), from Proto-Indo-European *ster-.
From Middle English star, ster, from Old English stær (“starling”), from Proto-Germanic *starô (“starling”), from Proto-Indo-European *stor- (“starling”).

stargazer.g: Someone who gazes at the stars; an astronomer or astrologer (now especially an amateur one).

starry.e: From Middle English sterry, equivalent to star + -y.

start.e: From Middle English stert, from the verb sterten (“to start, startle”).

From Middle English sterten (“to leap up suddenly, rush out”), from Old English styrtan (“to leap up, start”), from Proto-West Germanic *sturtijan (“to startle, move, set in motion”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ter- (“to be stiff”).

startle.e: From Middle English startlen (“to rush, jump”), from Old English steartlian (“to kick with the foot, struggle, stumble”), equivalent to start + -le.
startle.g: To move suddenly, or be excited, on feeling alarm; to start.

starve.e: From Middle English sterven (“to die, perish”), from Old English steorfan (“to die, perish”), from Proto-West Germanic *sterban, from Proto-Germanic *sterbaną (“to become stiff, die”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)terp- (“to lose strength, become numb, be motionless”); or from Proto-Indo-European *sterbʰ- (“to become stiff”), from *ster- (“stiff”).
starve.g: To die because of lack of food or of not eating.

state.e: From Middle English stat (as a noun); adopted c. 1200 from both Old French estat and Latin stātus (“manner of standing, attitude, position, carriage, manner, dress, apparel; and other senses”), from stāre (“to stand”). The sense of "polity" develops in the 14th century.
state.g: A condition; a set of circumstances applying at any given time.

stately.e: From Middle English staately, staatly, stateli, statelie, stately, statelyche, statelye, statli, statly. By surface analysis, state + -ly (adjectival suffix).
From Middle English stately, statli, equivalent to state + -ly (adverbial suffix).

statement.e: Back-formation from statementing or back-formation from statemented.
statement.g: To provide an official document of a proposition, especially in the UK, a Statement of Special Educational Needs.

station.e: From Middle English stacioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman estation, from Latin statiōnem, accusative of statiō (“standing, post, job, position”), whence also Italian stazione.

statue.e: From Old French statue, from Latin statua, derived from statuō (“set up or erect”).
statue.g: A three-dimensional work of art, usually representing a person or animal, usually created by sculpting, carving, molding, or casting.

stature.e: From Middle English stature, from Old French stature, from Latin statūra.
stature.g: A person or animal's natural height when standing upright.

statute.e: From Middle English statut, from Old French statut, from Late Latin statutum (“a statute”), neuter singular of Latin statutus, past participle of statuō (“to set up, establish”).
statute.g: A written law or ordinance passed by a legislative body.

stave.e: Back-formation from staves, the plural of staff.
stave.g: One of a number of narrow strips of wood, or narrow iron plates, placed edge to edge to form the sides, covering, or lining of a vessel or s

stay.e: From Middle English steyen, staien, from Old French estayer, estaier (“to fix, prop up, support, stay”), from estaye, estaie (“a prop, stay”), from Middle Dutch staeye (“a prop, stay”), a contracted form of staede, stade (“a prop, stay, help, aid”) (compare Middle Dutch staeyen, staeden (“to make firm, stay, support, hold still, stabilise”)).
stay.g: To remain in a particular place, especially for a definite or short period of time; sojourn; abide.

stay.e: From Middle English stay, from Old French estaye, estaie (“a prop, a stay”), from Middle Dutch staeye (“a prop, stay”), a contracted form of staede, stade ("a prop, stay, help, aid"; compare Middle Dutch staeyen, staeden (“to make firm, stay, support, hold still, stabilise”)), from Old Dutch *stad (“a site, place, location, standing”).

stead.e: From Middle English sted, stede (noun) and steden (verb), from Old English stede, from Proto-Germanic *stadiz (“place”), from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis (“standing, location”).
stead.g: The position or function (of someone or something), as taken on by a successor.
One's partner in a romantic relationship.

steadfast.e: From Middle English stedefast, from Old English stedefæst, from Proto-Germanic *stadifastuz, equivalent to stead (“place; spot; position”) + fast (“firm; fixed”).

steady.e: From Middle English stedy, studi, stidiȝ, perhaps continuing Old English stæþþiġ, ġestæþþiġ (“steadfast, stable, firm, staid”), equivalent to stead + -y; or calquing Middle Low German or Middle Dutch stēdig. Adjective sense 8 is a semantic loan from Singapore Hokkien 在 (chāi, “confident, skilled”, literally “steady”).
steady.g: Firm in standing or position; not tottering or shaking; fixed; firm.

steal.e: From Middle English stelen, from Old English stelan, from Proto-West Germanic *stelan, from Proto-Germanic *stelaną. For the meaning development compare with Russian красть (krastʹ, “to steal”) and Russian кра́сться (krástʹsja, “to stalk, to prowl, to slink”).
steal.g: To take illegally, or without the owner's permission, something owned by someone else without intending to return it.

stealth.e: From Middle English stelthe, from Old English stǣlþ, from Proto-Germanic *stēliþō, to Proto-Germanic *stelaną (“to steal, to sneak”) + *-iþō, equivalent to steal + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
stealth.g: The attribute or characteristic of acting in secrecy, or in such a way that the actions are unnoticed or difficult to detect by others.

stedfastness.e: From Middle English stedfastnes, stedfastnesse (“firmness of purpose; fortitude; loyalty, fidelity; strength, boldness, courage”), from Old English stedefæstnes (“constancy”); equivalent to stedfast + -ness.

steed.e: From Middle English stede (“steed”), from Old English stēda (“stallion, stud”), from Proto-West Germanic *stōdijō; (compare Old Dutch stoti (“herd of horses”), Old High German stuot (“herd of horses”)).
steed.g: A stallion, especially one used for riding.

steel.e: From Middle English stele, stel, from Old English stīele, from Proto-West Germanic *stahlī (“something made of steel”), enlargement of *stahl (“steel”), from Proto-Germanic *stahlą, from *stah- or *stag- (“to be firm, rigid”), from Proto-Indo-European *stak- (“to stay, to be firm”).
steel.g: An artificial metal produced from iron, harder and more elastic than elemental iron; used figuratively as a symbol of hardness.

steep.e: From Middle English steep, from Old English stēap (“high”), from Proto-Germanic *staupaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp- (“to push, stick”). The Proto-Indo-European root (and related) has many and varied descendants, including English stub; compare also Scots stap (“to strike, to forcibly insert”). The sense of “sharp slope” is attested circa 1200.
steep.g: Of a near-vertical gradient; of a slope, surface, curve, etc. that proceeds upward or downward at an angle approaching vertical.

steep.e: From Middle English stepen, from Old Norse steypa (“to make stoop, cast down, pour out, cast (metal)”), from Proto-Germanic *staupijaną (“to tumble, make tumble, plunge”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewb- (“to push, hit”).

steer.e: From Middle English steeren, steren, stiren, sturen, steoren, from Old English stēoran, stīeran, stȳran (“to steer; guide a vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *stiurijan (“to steer”), from Proto-Germanic *stiurijaną (“to steer”).
steer.g: To guide the course of a vessel, vehicle, aircraft etc. (by means of a device such as a rudder, paddle, or steering wheel).

steer.e: From Middle English steer, ster, from Old English stēor (“a young bull or cow; steer”), from Proto-Germanic *steuraz (“bull; steer”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)táwros (“wild bull; aurochs”).
steer.g: The castrated male of cattle, especially one raised for beef production.

stem.e: From Middle English stem, stemme, stempne, stevin, from Old English stemn (“stem”), from Proto-West Germanic *stamni, from Proto-Germanic *stamniz (“stem, tree stalk”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand, stay”).
stem.g: The stock of a family; a race or generation of progenitors.

stem.e: From Middle English stemmen, a borrowing from Old Norse stemma (“to stop, stem, dam”) (whence Danish stemme/stæmme (“to stem, dam up”)), from Proto-Germanic *stammijaną.
stem.g: To stop, hinder (for instance, a river or blood).

stench.e: From Middle English stench, from Old English stenċ (“stench, odor, fragrance”), from Proto-Germanic *stankwiz (“smell, fragrance, odor”), from Proto-Indo-European *stengʷ- (“to push, thrust”).
stench.g: a strong foul smell; a stink.

step.e: From Middle English steppen, from Old English steppan (“to step, go, proceed, advance”), stepe (“step”), from Proto-West Germanic *stappjan, from Proto-Germanic *stapjaną (“to step”), *stapiz (“step”), from Proto-Indo-European *stebʰ- (“to support, stomp, curse, be amazed”).
step.g: An advance or movement made from one foot to the other; a pace.

stern.e: From Middle English stern, sterne, sturne, from Old English styrne (“stern, grave, strict, austere, hard, severe, cruel”), from Proto-Germanic *sturnijaz (“angry, astonished, shocked”), from Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“rigid, stiff”).
stern.g: Having a hardness and severity of nature or manner.

stern.e: From Middle English sterne, likely from Old Norse stjórn (“control, steering”), related to stýra (“to steer”), from Proto-Germanic *stiurijaną, whence also English steer. The sense referring to a management post alludes to the fact that a sailing ship's captain would often stand on an aft deck.
stern.g: The rear part (after end) of a ship or other vessel.

sternly.e: From Middle English sternly, sternely, sterneliche, sturnely, sturneliche, from Old English stirnlīċe, styrnlīċe, stiernlīċe (“harshly; severely; sternly”), equivalent to stern + -ly.

stew.e: From Middle English stewe, stue, from Anglo-Norman estouve, Old French estuve (“bath, bathhouse”) (modern French étuve), from Medieval Latin stupha, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *extufāre, from ex- + Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos, “smoke, steam”), from τύφω (túphō, “to smoke”).
stew.g: A cooking-dish used for boiling; a cauldron.

stew.e: From Middle English stewen, stuwen, from the noun above; and also from Middle English stiven, styven (“to bathe, cook, stew”).
stew.g: To cook (food) by slowly boiling or simmering.

steward.e: From Middle English steward, stiward, from Old English stiġweard (“steward, housekeeper, one who has the superintendence of household affairs, guardian”), from stiġ (“a wooden enclosure; house, hall”) + weard (“ward, guard, guardian, keeper”), equivalent to sty + ward.
steward.g: A person who manages the property or affairs for another entity.

stewardship.e: From Middle English stiwardshepe, equivalent to steward + -ship.
stewardship.g: The rank or office of a steward.

stick.e: From Middle English sticke, stik, stikke (“branch, twig; kindling; mast; pale; stick, stylus”), from Old English sticca (“stick; peg; beam, rod”), from Proto-West Germanic *stikkō, from Proto-Germanic *stikkô (“pole, stick”), from *stikkōną (“to fix, stick”), from *stikaną (“to stick; to stab”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to be sharp; to sting”).
stick.g: An elongated piece of wood or similar material, typically put to some use, for example as a wand or baton.

stick.e: From Middle English stiken (“to stick, pierce, stab, remain embedded, be fastened”), from Old English stician (“to pierce, stab, remain embedded, be fastened”), from Proto-West Germanic *stikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *stikkōną (“to pierce, prick, be sharp”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tig-, *(s)teyg- (“to pierce, prick, be sharp”).
stick.g: A thrust with a pointed instrument; a stab; an instance of sticking (pricking or piercing).

stiff.e: From Middle English stiff, stiffe, stif, from Old English stīf, from Proto-West Germanic *stīf, from Proto-Germanic *stīfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *steypós. The expected Modern English form would be /staɪf/; /stɪf/ is probably originally from compounds such as stiffly, where the vowel was shortened before a consonant cluster.

stiff-necked.e: From stiff + neck + -ed. (figurative): Calque of Hebrew קשה ערף (Exodus 33). A biblical term similar to Swedish styvnackad, Ancient Greek σκληροτράχηλος (sklērotrákhēlos), Russian жестоковыйный (žestokovyjnyj), German halsstarrig etc.
stiff-necked.g: Having a stiff neck; suffering from torticollis

stiffen.e: From Middle English stifnen, equivalent to stiff + -en.

stifle.e: Perhaps derived from Middle English stuffen (“to kill by suffocation; to stifle from heat; to extinguish, suppress (body heat, breath, humour, etc.); to deprive a plant of the conditions necessary for growth, choke”) + -len (frequentative suffix). Stuffen is derived from Old French estofer, estouffer (“to choke, strangle, suffocate.
stifle.g: To make (an animal or person) unconscious or cause (an animal or person) to die by preventing breathing; to smother, to suffocate.

still.e: From Middle English stille (“motionless, stationary”), from Old English stille (“still, quiet”), from Proto-West Germanic *stillī, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)telH- (“to be silent; to be still”).
Aphetic form of distil, or from Latin stillare.

sting.e: From Middle English styng, sting, stynge, stenge, from Old English sting, stincg (“a sting, stab, thrust made with a pointed instrument; the wound made by a stab or sting”), from Proto-Germanic *stingaz; possibly also from Old English stynġ, from Proto-Germanic *stungiz.
sting.g: A bump left on the skin after having been stung.

sting.e: From Middle English stingen, from Old English stingan, from Proto-Germanic *stinganą.
sting.g: To hurt, usually by introducing poison or a sharp point, or both.

stinger.e: From sting + -er. Both figurative and literal senses appeared in the 16th century.
stinger.g: A pointed portion of an insect or arachnid used for attack.

stinging.e: From Middle English styngyng; equivalent to sting + -ing.

stingy.e: Uncertain, possibly from stinge, a dialectal variation of sting (verb).
stingy.g: Unwilling to spend, give, or share; ungenerous; mean.

stink.e: From Middle English stinken, from Old English stincan, from Proto-Germanic *stinkwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *stengʷ-, *stegʷ- (“to push, thrust, strike”).
stink.g: To have a strong bad smell.

stinking.e: From Middle English stynkynge, stinkinge, stinkinde, stinkende, stynkande, stynkand, from Old English stincende, from Proto-Germanic *stinkwandz (“stinking”), present participle of Proto-Germanic *stinkwaną (“to stink”), equivalent to stink + -ing.

stir.e: From Middle English stiren, sturien, steren, from Old English styrian (“to be in motion, move, agitate, stir, disturb, trouble”), from Proto-Germanic *sturiz (“turmoil, noise, confusion”), related to Proto-West Germanic *staurijan (“to destroy, disturb”).
stir.g: To disturb the relative position of the particles (of a liquid or similar) by passing an object through it.

stir.e: From Romani stariben (“prison”), nominalisation of (a)star (“seize”), causative of ast (“remain”), probably from Sanskrit आतिष्ठति (ātiṣṭhati, “stand or remain by”), from तिष्ठति (tiṣṭhati, “stand”).

stock.e: From Middle English stok, from Old English stocc, from Proto-West Germanic *stokk, from Proto-Germanic *stukkaz (“tree-trunk”). Modern senses are mostly referring either to the trunk from which the tree grows (figuratively, its origin and/or support/foundation), or to a piece of wood, stick, or rod.

stock.g: A thrust with a rapier; a stoccado.

stoke.e: From Middle English stoken, from Middle Dutch stoken (“to poke, thrust”) or Middle Low German stoken (“to poke, thrust”), from Old Dutch *stokon or Old Saxon *stokon, both from Proto-West Germanic *stokōn, from Proto-Germanic *stukōną (“to be stiff, push”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewg- (“to push, beat”).

From a back-formation of stoker, apparently from Dutch stoker, from stoken (“to kindle a fire, incite, instigate”), from Middle Dutch stoken (“to poke, thrust”), from stock (“stick, stock”), see: tandenstoker. Ultimately the same word as above.
stoke.g: To feed, stir up, especially, a fire or furnace.

stole.e: From Old English stole, from Latin stola, from Ancient Greek στολή (stolḗ, “stole, garment, equipment”); akin to stall.
stole.g: A garment consisting of a decorated band worn on the back of the neck, each end hanging over the chest, worn in ecclesiastical settings or s

stolen.e: From Middle English stolen, istolen, from Old English stolen, ġestolen, from Proto-Germanic *stulanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *stelaną (“to steal”), equivalent to stole + -en.

stomach.e: From Middle English stomak, from Old French estomac, from Latin stomachus, from Ancient Greek στόμαχος (stómakhos), from στόμα (stóma, “mouth”). Partially displaced native Old English maga, whence Modern English maw.
stomach.g: An organ in animals that stores food in the process of digestion.

stomacher.e: From Middle English stomakere, stomachere, perhaps after Anglo-Norman *estomachier. Equivalent to stomach + -er.

stone.e: From Middle English ston, stone, stan, from Old English stān, from Proto-West Germanic *stain, from Proto-Germanic *stainaz (“stone”), from Proto-Indo-European *steyh₂- (“to stiffen”).
stone.g: A hard earthen substance that can form rocks; especially, such substance when regarded as a building material.

stone.e: From Middle English stonen, stanen, from Old English *stānian (“to stone”), from Proto-West Germanic *stainōn, from Proto-Germanic *stainōną (“to stone”).
stone.g: To pelt with stones; especially, to kill by pelting with stones.

stonecutter.g: Somebody who cuts, carves or dresses stone.

stoned.e: From Middle English stoned (simple past) and stoned, istoned (past participle), equivalent to stone + -ed. The etymology for the sense of "exhilarated, intoxicated by substances", which originated in American English in the mid-20th century, is not fully clear.

stony.e: From Middle English stony, stoni, stani, from Old English stāniġ, stǣniġ (“stony, rocky”), from Proto-Germanic *stainagaz (“stony”), equivalent to stone + -y.

stool.e: From Middle English stool, from Old English stōl (“chair, seat”), from Proto-West Germanic *stōl, from Proto-Germanic *stōlaz (“chair”), from Proto-Indo-European *stoh₂los (“frame, rack, stand”), from *steh₂- (“to stand”).
stool.g: A seat, especially for one person and without armrests.
Alternative form of stole (“plant from which layers are propagated by bending its branches into the soil; stolon.”).

stoop.e: From Middle English stoupen, from Old English stūpian (“to bow, bend”), from Proto-West Germanic *stūpōn, from Proto-Germanic *stūpōną, *stūpijaną (“to stand out”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewb- (“to push, butt, knock”). Related also to Old Frisian stēpa (“to help”), Old Norse steypa (“to cause to stoop, cast down, overthrow”).
stoop.g: A stooping, bent position of the body.

stoop.e: From Middle English stope, stoupe, from Old Norse staup (“dip, well, cup”), from Proto-Germanic *staupą, related to the verb *staupijaną (“to steep”).
stoop.g: A vessel for holding liquids; like a flagon but without the spout.

stop.e: From Middle English stoppen, stoppien, from Old English stoppian (“to stop, close”), from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn, from Proto-Germanic *stuppōną (“to stop, close”), *stuppijaną (“to push, pierce, prick”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp-, *(s)tewb- (“to push; stick”), from *(s)tew- (“to bump; impact; butt; push; beat; strike; hit”).
From Middle English stoppe, from Old English stoppa (“bucket, pail, a stop”), from Proto-Germanic *stuppô (“vat, vessel”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teub- (“to push, hit; stick, stump”).

stopped.e: From stop + -ed. In some senses, the adjective follows from the verb; in others, it may derive directly from the noun stop.
stopped.g: Not moving, but not properly parked or berthed; said also of the occupants of such a vehicle.

store.e: From Middle English store, borrowed from Anglo-Norman stor, from Latin īnstaurāre, from īnstaurō + -āre.
store.g: A place where items may be accumulated or routinely kept.

stork.e: From Middle English stork, from Old English storc, from Proto-West Germanic *stork, from Proto-Germanic *sturkaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sr̥ǵos (“stork”). Near cognates include Dutch stork, German Storch, Swedish stork, and Icelandic storkur.
stork.g: A large wading bird with long legs and a long beak of the order Ciconiiformes and its family Ciconiidae.

storm.e: From Middle English storm (“disturbed state of the atmosphere; heavy precipitation; battle, conflict; attack”), from Old English storm (“tempest, storm; attack; storm of arrows; disquiet, disturbance, tumult, uproar; onrush, rush”), from Proto-West Germanic *sturm (“storm”), from Proto-Germanic *sturmaz (“storm”).
storm.g: Any disturbed state of the atmosphere causing destructive or unpleasant weather, especially one affecting the earth's surface involving stro

storm.e: The Middle English word did not survive into modern English.
storm.g: Preceded by the dummy subject it: to have strong winds and usually lightning and thunder, and/or hail, rain, or snow.

stormy.e: From Middle English stormy, stormi, from Old English *stormiġ (“stormy”), equivalent to storm + -y.

story.e: From Middle English storie, storye, from Anglo-Norman estorie by aphesis, from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ῐ̔στορῐ́ᾱ (hĭstorĭ́ā, “learning through research”).
story.g: An account of real or fictional events.

story.e: Alternative form of what's the story (“how are you?”)
story.g: Used as a greeting, short for what's the story?

stout.e: From Middle English stoute, from Old French estout (“brave, fierce, proud”) (Modern French dialectal stout (“proud”)), from earlier Old French estolt (“strong”), from Frankish *stolt, *stult (“bold, proud”), from Proto-Germanic *stultaz (“bold, proud”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, stand”).
From Middle English stouten, from the adjective (see above).

straggler.g: Someone who goes against the direct or proper course, or from the company to which they belong.

straight.e: From Middle English streight, streght, streiȝt, the past participle of strecchen (“to stretch”), from Old English streċċan (past participle ġestreaht, ġestreht), from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan (“to stretch”). Equivalent to stretch + -ed. In some senses, conflated with strait (“narrow, constricted”), which is from Latin strictus via Old French estreit.
straight.g: Not crooked, curly, or bent; having a constant direction throughout its length.

straightway.g: A straight section of a racetrack.
Synonym of straightaway or straight away (“at once, immediately”).

strain.e: From Middle English streen, strene, streon, istreon (“race, stock, generation”), from Old English strēon, ġestrēon (“gain, wealth”), from Proto-West Germanic *streun, from Proto-Germanic *streuną (“heap, treasure, profit, gain”).
From Middle English straynen, streinen, streynen, from Old French estreindre (whence French étreindre (“to grip”)), from Latin stringō (“to draw tight together, to tie”).

strait.e: From Middle English streit, from Old French estreit (modern form étroit), from Latin strictus, perfect passive participle of stringō (“compress, tighten”).
strait.g: Narrow; restricted as to space or room; close.

straitness.g: The state or quality of being strait.

strake.e: From Middle English strake, from Old English *straca (> Anglo-Latin straca), from Proto-West Germanic *strakō, from Proto-Germanic *strakaz (“straight”).
strake.g: An iron fitting of a traditional wooden wheel, such as a hub component or bearing (e.g., box, bushel), a cleat, or a rim covering.

strand.e: From Middle English strand, strond, from Old English strand (“strand, sea-shore, shore”), from Proto-West Germanic *strand, from Proto-Germanic *strandō (“edge, rim, shore”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)trAnt- (“strand, border, field”), from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to broaden, spread out”).
strand.g: The shore or beach of the sea or ocean.

strand.e: Origin uncertain. Perhaps the same as strand ("rivulet, stream, gutter"; see Etymology 1 above); or from Middle English *stran, from Old French estran (“a rope, cord”), from Middle High German stren, strene (“skein, strand”), from Old High German streno, from Proto-West Germanic *strenō, from Proto-Germanic *strinô (“strip, strand”).
strand.g: Each of the strings which, twisted together, make up a yarn, rope or cord.

strange.e: From Middle English straunge, strange, stronge, from Old French estrange, from Latin extrāneus (“that which is on the outside”). Largely displaced native fremd, selcouth, and uncouth, from Old English fremede, seldcūþ, and uncūþ.
strange.g: Not normal; odd, unusual, surprising, out of the ordinary, often with a negative connotation.

strangely.e: From Middle English straungely (“strangely, aloofly, intricately”); equivalent to strange + -ly.
strangely.g: In a strange or coincidental manner.

stranger.e: From Middle English straunger, from Old French estrangier (“foreign, alien”), from estrange, from Latin extraneus (“foreign, external”) (whence also English estrange), from extra (“outside of”).
stranger.g: A person whom one does not know; a person who is neither a friend nor an acquaintance.

strangle.e: From Middle English stranglen, from Old French estrangler, from Latin strangulō, strangulāre, from Ancient Greek στραγγαλόομαι (strangalóomai, “to be strangled”), from στραγγάλη (strangálē, “a halter”); compare στραγγός (strangós, “twisted”) and string.
strangle.g: To kill someone by squeezing the throat so as to cut off the oxygen supply.

strap.e: From a variant of earlier strope (“loop on a harness”), from Middle English strope, stroppe, from Late Old English strop, stropp (“a band, thong, strap; oar-thong”) and Old French estrope (“strap, loop on a harness”), both from Latin stroppus, struppus (“strap”), from Ancient Greek στρόφος (stróphos, “rope”) (compare strophe).
strap.g: A long, narrow, pliable strip of leather, cloth, or the like.

strategy.e: From Latin stratēgia, from Ancient Greek στρατηγία (stratēgía, “office of general, command, generalship”), from στρατηγός (stratēgós, “the leader or commander of an army, a general”), from στρατός (stratós, “army”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead, conduct”).
strategy.g: The science and art of military command as applied to the overall planning and conduct of warfare.

straw.e: From Middle English straugh, strauȝ, straw, strawe, strea, streuw, from Old English strēaw, strēow, from Proto-West Germanic *strau, from Proto-Germanic *strawą (“that which is strewn, straw”), from Proto-Indo-European *strew- (“to spread, strew”), from *sterh₃- (“to extend, spread”), from *ster- (“barren, infertile”).
straw.g: A dried stalk of a cereal plant.

stray.e: From Middle English stray, strey, from Anglo-Norman estray, stray, Old French estrai, from the verb (see below).
stray.g: Any domestic animal that lacks an enclosure, proper place, or company, but that instead wanders at large or is lost; an estray.

stray.e: From Middle English strayen, partly from Old French estraier, from Vulgar Latin via strata, and partly from Middle English strien, streyen, streyȝen (“to spread, scatter”), from Old English strēġan (“to strew”).
stray.g: To wander, as from a direct course; to deviate, or go out of the way.

streak.e: From Middle English streke, from Old English strica, from Proto-Germanic *strikiz, from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“line”).
streak.g: An irregular line, as is left from smearing or motion.

stream.e: From Middle English streem, strem, from Old English strēam, from Proto-West Germanic *straum, from Proto-Germanic *straumaz (“stream”), from Proto-Indo-European *srowmos (“river”), from Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow”).
stream.g: A small river; a large creek; a body of moving water confined by banks.

streaming.e: From Middle English stremyng, stremynge, stremande, equivalent to stream + -ing.
streaming.g: Flowing or moving in continuous succession, like fluid in a stream.

street.e: From Middle English strete, from Anglian Old English strēt (“street”, compare West Saxon Old English strǣt) from Proto-West Germanic *strātu (“street”), an early borrowing from Late Latin (via) strāta (“paved (road)”), from Latin strātus, past participle of sternō (“stretch out, spread, bestrew with, cover, pave”).
street.g: A paved part of road, usually in a village or a town.

strength.e: From Middle English strengthe, from Old English strengþu (“strength”), from Proto-West Germanic *strangiþu (“strongness; strength”), equivalent to strong + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
strength.g: The quality or degree of being strong.

strengthen.e: From rare Middle English strengthenen (14th c.), from earlier strengthen (12th c.), where -en is the infinitive ending. Probably the original form was reinterpreted as strength + -en around the time when the infinitive ending was being apocopated in late Middle English.
strengthen.g: To make strong or stronger; to add strength to; to increase the strength of; to fortify.

stress.e: From a shortening of Middle English destresse, borrowed from Old French destrecier, from Latin distringō (“to stretch out”). This form probably coalesced with Middle English stresse, from Old French estrece (“narrowness”), from Vulgar Latin *strictia, from Latin strictus (“narrow”).
stress.g: A physical, chemical, infective agent aggressing an organism.

stretch.e: From Middle English strecchen, from Old English streċċan (“to stretch, hold out, extend, spread out, prostrate”), from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan (“to stretch, make taut or tight”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)treg-, *streg-, *treg- (“stiff, rigid”).

stretching.e: From Middle English strecchinge, strecchynge, from Old English streċċende, from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjandī, present participle of *strakkjan (“to stretch”), equivalent to stretch + -ing.
stretching.g: Requiring a high level of effort or performance.

stricken.e: From Middle English striken, ystriken, from Old English stricen, ġestricen, from Proto-West Germanic *strikan, from Proto-Germanic *strikanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *strīkaną (“to strike”).

strict.e: Borrowed from Latin strictus, past participle of stringere (“to draw tight, bind, contract”).

stride.e: From Middle English striden, from Old English strīdan (“stride”), from Proto-West Germanic *strīdan, from Proto-Germanic *strīdaną.
From Middle English stride, stryde, from Old English stride (“a stride, pace”), from the verb (see above).

strife.e: From Middle English strif, stryf, striffe, from Old French estrif, noun derived from estriver, from Frankish *strīban; compare Dutch strijven.

strike.e: From Middle English stryken, from Old English strīcan, from Proto-West Germanic *strīkan, from Proto-Germanic *strīkaną, from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to stroke, rub, press”).
strike.g: To delete or cross out; to scratch or eliminate.

string.e: From Middle English string, streng, strynge, from Old English strenġ, from Proto-West Germanic *strangi, from Proto-Germanic *strangiz (“string”), from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“rope, cord, strand; to tighten”).
string.g: A long, thin and flexible structure made from threads twisted together.

string.e: From Middle English stryngen, strengen, from the noun (see above).

stringed.e: From Middle English strynged, y-strenged, equivalent to string + -ed.

strip.e: From alteration of stripe or from Middle Low German strippe, of uncertain ultimate origin, perhaps derived from a lost strong verb Proto-Germanic *strīpaną, with no clear cognates outside of Germanic except for Irish sríab (“line, stripe”).
strip.g: A long, thin piece of land; any long, thin area.

strip.e: From Middle English strepen, strippen, from Old English strīepan (“plunder”), from Proto-Germanic *strēpōną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ter(h₁)- (“to be stiff; be rigid; exert”). Probably related to German Strafe (“deprivation, fine, punishment”).
strip.g: To remove or take away, often in strips or stripes.

stripe.e: From Middle English stripe, strype, from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German strîpe, from Proto-West Germanic *strīpā, *strīpō, from Proto-Germanic *strīpô.
stripe.g: A long region of a single colour in a repeating pattern of similar regions.

stripling.e: From Middle English stripling (“an adolescent, a youth (specifically one who is male); a child”), possibly from strepen (“to remove the clothes of, undress, strip; to peel off; to skin (an animal); to remove; to take something away from someone.
stripling.g: A young man in the state of adolescence, or just passing from boyhood to manhood; a lad. .

strive.e: From Middle English striven (“to strive”), from Old French estriver (“to compete, quarrel”), from Frankish *strīban (“to exert, make an effort”) from Proto-Germanic *strībaną, or from Frankish *stribēn (“to strive”) from Proto-Germanic *stribāną.
strive.g: To try to achieve a result; to make strenuous effort; to try earnestly and persistently.

stroke.e: Sense 3.5.2.2 (“the oblique, slash, or virgule (‘/’)”) is a contraction of oblique stroke, a variant of oblique which was originally used in telegraphy.
stroke.g: An act of hitting; a blow, a hit.

stroll.e: Borrowed from German strollen, seemingly from Alemannic German strollen; related to Strolch (“vagabond; rascal”) and strolchen.
stroll.g: A wandering on foot; an idle and leisurely walk; a ramble; a saunter.

strong.e: From Middle English strong, strang, from Old English strang (“strong”), from Proto-West Germanic *strang (“severe, strict, rigorous, strong”), from Proto-Germanic *strangaz (“tight, strict, straight, strong”), from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“taut, stiff, tight”).
strong.g: Capable of producing great physical force.

stronghold.e: From Middle English stranghalde, strong-hold, strong-holde, from strong (“having physical strength, sturdy, strong; built to withstand assaults, fortified”) (from Old English strang, strong (“strong”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“stiff, tight”)) + hōld (“grasp, grip; control, possession, rule”) (from Old English).
stronghold.g: A place built to withstand attack; a fortress.

strongly.e: From Middle English strongly, from Old English stranglīċe (“strongly”), equivalent to strong + -ly.
strongly.g: In a strong or powerful manner.

structure.e: From Middle French structure, from Latin structūra (“a fitting together, adjustment, building, erection, a building, edifice, structure”), from struere, past participle structus (“pile up, arrange, assemble, build”).
structure.g: A cohesive whole built up of distinct parts.

struggle.e: From Middle English struglen, stroglen, strogelen, of obscure origin; perhaps from a variant of *strokelen, *stroukelen (> English stroll), from Middle Dutch struyckelen ("to stumble, trip, falter"; > Modern Dutch struikelen), the frequentative form of Old Dutch *strūkon (“to stumble”), from Proto-Germanic *strūkōną, *strūkēną (“to be stiff”).
struggle.g: An effortful attempt to escape something dangerous, usually out of fear for one's life or health.

strum.g: To play (a guitar or other stringed instrument) by plucking various strings simultaneously.

strut.e: The English word is cognate with Danish strutte (“to bulge, bristle”), Low German strutt (“stiff”), Middle High German striuzen (“to bristle; to ruffle”) (modern German strotzen (“to bristle up”), sträußen (obsolete, except in Alemannic)); and compare Gothic 𐌸𐍂𐌿𐍄𐍃𐍆𐌹𐌻𐌻 (þrutsfill, “leprosy”), Old Norse þrútinn (“swollen”).
strut.g: Of a peacock or other fowl: to stand or walk stiffly, with the tail erect and spread out.

strut.e: Probably an archaic past participle of strut (“to (cause something to) bulge, protrude, or swell”), now replaced by strutted: see etymology 1.
strut.g: Swelling out due to being full; bulging, protuberant, swollen.

stub.e: From Middle English stubbe (“tree stump”), from Old English stybb, stubb (“tree stump”), from Proto-West Germanic *stubb, from Proto-Germanic *stubbaz (compare Middle Dutch stubbe, Old Norse stubbr, Faroese stubbi (“stub”)), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tew-; compare steep (“sharp slope”). Sense extended in Middle English to similarly shaped objects.
stub.g: Something blunted, stunted, or cut short, such as stubble or a stump.

stubble.e: From Middle English stuble, from Anglo-Norman stuble, estuble, from Old French estoble, esteule (whence Modern French éteule), from Latin stipula (“stalk, straw”).
stubble.g: Short, coarse hair, especially on a man’s face.

stubborn.e: From Middle English stiborne, stibourne, stoburn, stoburne, styburne, stiborn, of uncertain origin; one hypothesis is that it may be from Old English *stybbor, from Old English stybb (“a stump, stub”) + -or (adjective-formation suffix, as in bitor, whence English bitter).
stubborn.g: Refusing to move or to change one's opinion; obstinate; firmly resisting; persistent in doing something.

stud.e: From Middle English stood, stod, from Old English stōd, from Proto-West Germanic *stōd, from Proto-Germanic *stōdą. The phonetic development is the same as in blood, flood, which unlike stud were not adapted orthographically.
stud.g: A male animal, especially a stud horse (stallion), kept for breeding.

stud.e: From Middle English stude, from Old English studu, from Proto-West Germanic *stuþ, from Proto-Germanic *stuþs.
stud.g: A small object that protrudes from something; an ornamental knob.

study.e: From Middle English studien, from Old French estudier (Modern French étudier), from estudie (noun), borrowed from Latin studium.
study.g: To review materials already learned in order to make sure one does not forget them, usually in preparation for an examination.

study.e: From Middle English studie, from Old French estudie (Modern French étude), borrowed from Latin studium (“zeal, dedication, study”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewd- (“to push, to hit”).
study.g: Mental effort to acquire knowledge or learning.

stuff.e: From Middle English stuf, stuffe, from Anglo-Latin stuffa and its etymon Old French estofe, estoffe, estuf, estuffe, stoffe, from estoffer, estofer (“to provide what is necessary, equip, stuff”), borrowed from Old High German stoffōn, from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn (“to clog up, block, fill”).
stuff.g: Miscellaneous items or objects; (with possessive) personal effects.

stuff.e: From Middle English stuffen (“to equip, furnish”), borrowed from Old French estoffer, estofer (“to provide what is necessary, equip, stuff”), borrowed from Old High German stoffōn, from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn (“to clog up, block, fill”).
stuff.g: To fill by packing or crowding something into; to cram with something; to load to excess.

stumble.e: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stam- (“to trip up; to stammer, stutter”), thereby related to German stumm (“mute”), Dutch stom (“dumb”).
stumble.g: A fall, trip or substantial misstep.

stump.e: From Middle English stumpe, stompe (“stump”), from or akin to Middle Low German stump (“stump”) or Middle Dutch stomp, from Old Saxon or Old Dutch *stump, from Proto-West Germanic *stump, from Proto-Germanic *stumpaz (“stump, blunt, part cut off”).
stump.g: The remains of something that has been cut off; especially the remains of a tree, the remains of a limb.

stun.e: From Middle English stonen, stone (“to astonish, stun, numb”, also stoneyen), probably either directly or indirectly from Anglo-Norman estoner (“to stun, astonish”), from Late Latin *stunāre, from Frankish *stunōn (“to thunder, crash”) or perhaps from an unattested Latin *extonāre (“to thunder out, make a thunderous sound”), from tonāre ("to thunder".
stun.g: To incapacitate; especially by inducing disorientation or unconsciousness.

stunt.e: From dialectal stunt (“stubborn, dwarfed”), from Middle English stont, stunt (“short, brief”), from Old English stunt (“stupid, foolish, simple”), from Proto-Germanic *stuntaz (“short, compact, stupid, dull”).
stunt.g: To check or hinder the growth or development of.

stupid.e: From Middle French stupide, from Latin stupidus (“struck senseless, amazed”), from stupeō (“be amazed or confounded, be struck senseless”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tup-, *(s)tewp- (“to push, stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”). Related also to Old English stoppian (“to block, stop”).

stupidity.e: From Latin stupiditātem, accusative of Latin stupiditās, equivalent to stupid + -ity.

stupor.e: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin stupor (“insensibility, numbness, dullness”). Distantly related (from Proto-Indo-European, via Proto-Germanic) to stint, stub, and steep.
stupor.g: A state of greatly dulled or completely suspended consciousness or sensibility; (particularly medicine) a chiefly mental condition marked by

stylus.e: Borrowed from Latin stylus (“a stake or pale”). Probably not directly related to Ancient Greek στῦλος (stûlos, “a pillar”).
stylus.g: An ancient writing implement consisting of a small rod with a pointed end for scratching letters on clay, wax-covered tablets or other surfa
